title: Cybersecurity Awareness Assessment
description: Fifteen questions across the six core topics. The result identifies which areas to focus on next.

levels.label: Beginner
levels.blurb: Start with the free modules in order. They cover the patterns behind most attacks aimed at remote workers.

levels.label: Intermediate
levels.blurb: You recognise the common attacks. The weak areas below are where a convincing attempt would still get through.

levels.label: Advanced
levels.blurb: Strong instincts across the board. Focus on the role-based scenarios, where attacks are tailored rather than generic.

questions.questionText: An email from your bank says your account will be suspended in 24 hours and asks you to scan a QR code to verify it. What is the strongest reason to distrust this?

options.text: QR codes cannot be used by real companies
Urgency plus an unsolicited QR code is a common way to bypass email link scanning
Banks never send email
The email arrived outside office hours

questions.explanation: Security filters scan text links, not images. Hiding the destination inside a QR code and adding a deadline is designed to get you to act before checking.

questions.questionText: A login page looks identical to your company portal and the address bar shows a padlock. Is it safe?

options.text: Yes, the padlock confirms it is the real site
Not necessarily, the padlock only means the connection is encrypted

questions.explanation: Anyone can get a certificate for a domain they own, including a lookalike one. The padlock says the connection is private, not that the site is legitimate.

questions.questionText: Which address is most likely a typosquat of microsoft.com?

options.text: support.microsoft.com
microsoft.com/support
micros0ft-verify.com
login.microsoftonline.com

questions.explanation: A zero replacing the letter o, plus an unrelated word joined by a hyphen. The real domain sits to the left of the final slash, not anywhere in the string.

questions.questionText: What separates spear phishing from ordinary phishing?

options.text: It is sent to far more people at once
It uses details about you, your work, or your clients to seem legitimate
It always contains an attachment
It only targets senior management

questions.explanation: The attacker researches you first, often from public profiles, so the message fits your actual work and lowers your guard.

questions.questionText: A file arrives named Invoice_Oct2026.pdf.exe. What does the double extension mean?

options.text: It is a PDF that opens in a special reader
It is a program disguised as a document
It is a compressed archive
Nothing, this is normal for invoices

questions.explanation: Only the final extension decides what the file is. The .pdf is part of the name, designed to be the bit you notice.

questions.questionText: A client you work with messages you on WhatsApp asking for a file to be sent urgently to a new address. What is the right first step?

options.text: Send it, since you recognise the client
Confirm through the channel you normally use with them before sending
Reply asking them to confirm it is really them
Send a lower quality version as a compromise

questions.explanation: Asking in the same channel proves nothing, since whoever controls it can just say yes. Verifying elsewhere is what makes the check meaningful.

questions.questionText: A text says a package could not be delivered and links to a shortened URL. Why are shortened links a particular problem on a phone?

options.text: They load more slowly on mobile data
They hide the real destination, and small screens make the address harder to inspect
They only work on Android
They cannot be opened in a browser

questions.explanation: The shortener hides where you are actually going, and a narrow address bar truncates what you could otherwise check.

questions.questionText: A text claiming to be from your bank asks you to reply with the verification code they just sent. Should you?

options.text: Yes, if the number matches the one on their website
No, a legitimate organisation never asks you to share a one time code

questions.explanation: The code exists to prove it is you. Anyone asking for it is trying to complete a login they started. Caller and sender IDs can be spoofed, so a matching number proves nothing.

questions.questionText: Someone calls saying they are from IT, that your account is compromised, and asks you to approve the login prompt on your phone. What is happening?

options.text: Routine security maintenance
They are trying to log in as you and need you to approve it
A test of the alert system
A network fault needing confirmation

questions.explanation: That prompt appeared because someone entered your password. Approving it completes their login. Real IT does not need you to approve a sign in they did not make.

questions.questionText: An unexpected caller asks you to install AnyDesk so they can fix a problem. What is the risk?

options.text: It uses a lot of bandwidth
It gives the caller direct control of your machine and whatever you are signed into
It is not compatible with Windows
It voids your warranty

questions.explanation: Remote access tools are legitimate, which is what makes them effective here. Once connected, the caller can act as you, including in any session you have open.

questions.questionText: What makes pretexting different from a one off phishing email?

options.text: It always happens by phone
It builds a believable role and relationship over time before asking for anything
It only targets large companies
It relies on malware rather than conversation

questions.explanation: The attacker invests in being credible first. By the time the request arrives it feels like a reasonable next step from someone you already know.

questions.questionText: Someone claiming to be an external auditor asks for employee records and resists using the ticketing system. What does that resistance suggest?

options.text: They are busy and working efficiently
They are avoiding a process that would create a record and verify who they are
The ticketing system is probably down
Auditors normally work outside official channels

questions.explanation: Official channels confirm identity and leave a trail. Someone steering you away from them is avoiding exactly that.

questions.questionText: Which form of multi-factor authentication is strongest?

options.text: Codes sent by SMS
An authenticator app or hardware security key
Security questions
A longer password

questions.explanation: SMS can be intercepted or redirected through a SIM swap. App based codes and hardware keys stay on a device you hold.

options.text: Replying to the message to ask if it is genuine
Confirming the request through a different channel you already trust
Waiting 24 hours before acting
Forwarding it to a colleague for a second opinion

questions.explanation: If the request is fake, the channel it arrived on is controlled by the attacker. Using a number or account you already had is what makes the check independent.

questions.questionText: Select ALL that reduce the risk of a compromised home network. (Select all that apply)

options.text: Changing the router's default admin password
Putting smart home devices on a separate guest network
Hiding the network name so it is not broadcast
Turning off remote management on the router

questions.explanation: Default passwords are published, remote management exposes the router to the internet, and isolating IoT devices limits what a compromised one can reach. Hiding the network name does not stop anyone scanning for it.
